draft.title: Solving simple exponential equations
card: An exponential equation has the unknown in the index, such as 3ˣ = 81. The base is the number being raised to a power.
Write both sides as powers of the same base. Here 81 = 3⁴, so 3ˣ = 3⁴.
When the bases match, the indices must be equal. So x = 4.
If the index has more than x, set the indices equal and solve. For 2^(x + 1) = 32, write 32 = 2⁵, so x + 1 = 5 and x = 4.
draft.remember: Same base on both sides, then the indices are equal.

a.why: 125 = 5 × 5 × 5 = 5³, so 5ˣ = 5³ and x = 3. Choosing 25 comes from dividing 125 by 5, which does not give the index.

b.why: 64 = 2⁶, so x + 3 = 6 and x = 3. The tempting answer 6 forgets that the index is x + 3, not just x.
b.clue: Write 64 as a power of 2, then solve for the index.

final.title: Solving simple exponential equations
card: An exponential equation has the unknown in the index, such as \(3^{x} = 81\). The base is the number being raised to a power.
Write both sides as powers of the same base. Here \(81 = 3^{4}\), so \(3^{x} = 3^{4}\).
When the bases match, the indices must be equal. So \(x = 4\).
If the index has more than \(x\), set the indices equal and solve. For \(2^{x + 1} = 32\), write \(32 = 2^{5}\), so \(x + 1 = 5\) and \(x = 4\).
final.remember: Same base on both sides, then the indices are equal.

a.why: \(125 = 5 \times 5 \times 5 = 5^{3}\), so \(5^{x} = 5^{3}\) and \(x = 3\). Choosing 25 comes from dividing 125 by 5, which does not give the index.

b.why: \(64 = 2^{6}\), so \(x + 3 = 6\) and \(x = 3\). The tempting answer 6 forgets that the index is \(x + 3\), not just \(x\).
b.clue: Write 64 as a power of 2, then solve for the index.
